utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please, and let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you all. Appearances, Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: David Cunningham assisted by Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. First of all, I apologise for the delay with which we are starting. I know that time is precious today and tomorrow. Reason, as you know, was that the previous trial went beyond the anticipated quarter to 2.00 deadline which automatically entails a delay in starting on our part. So that was beyond my control, and my apologies to you. Second thing, we will need to stop at a certain point in time to do the Maglov Initial Appearance. I have been given to understand that there shouldn't be any problems, that everything should be plain sailing, and that the Initial Appearance shouldn't take long. Or perhaps even less than I anticipated. Only thing is we need to programme well so that there will be the least time wasted or usurped from the Brdjanin case. I think that is still possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told, if I can assist, that apart from the interpreters obviously needing a break, that there needs to be a break because of tapes being changed because it's a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my idea was this, Ms. Korner, that there will be the usual break at quarter to 4.00, and we'll start with Maglov immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that would be at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need 20 minutes. So 30 minutes will be very ideal for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we'll finish with that. If need be, there will be another break between Maglov and Brdjanin, but then there will be no further breaks. This is the idea. Usually in Brdjanin, you have two breaks in any case. So there will be two breaks in any case, except that perhaps we will lose 20 minutes or something like that. That's my -- what I am hoping for. And we play it by ear. Any preliminaries before we escort the usher in? Madam usher, please. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This is very brief, this witness, he is bilingual, he is going to attempt to testify in English. And I've told him if he feels uncomfortable, he can go back to his native language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to him. Your client needs to have interpretation in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I just wanted to inform the Chamber of that. And I've told the witness that even though we're going to try to do this in English, he needs to have space between his answers so it can be properly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. This is no protective measures, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how long do you expect your in-chief, or direct as you call it in the States, to last, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My examination will certainly finish today, probably in less than two hours. That would probably be my guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness comes in, can I ask a favour just -- no witnesses at the moment are being asked for their dates of birth for some reason. I wonder when they are asked to give their name, they could also be asked to give their dates of birth. There's a reason particularly with this witness because there's potentially a confusion between someone else of the same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are very right. Quite right, Ms. Korner. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll be glad to do that with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever you forget, I will that myself then, okay? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are a Defence witness in the trial instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin. And you are going to commence giving testimony within a few minutes. Before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath; namely, that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn declaration with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please, take a seat. And good afternoon once more. The procedure is a very simple one. You will first be asked questions by counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin, you being a Defence witness. And that will be Mr. Cunningham questioning you or examining you. After that, it will be followed by a cross-examination which will be conducted by Ms. Korner, who is the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case. Your duty or obligation or responsibility as a witness is to answer all questions truthfully and as fully as possible, but also concisely irrespective of who is putting the question. In other words, irrespective of whether it's the Defence, that have brought you here to give testimony, or the Prosecution that is putting questions to you. Now, your obligation is to answer each and every question the same. That is truthfully and as comprehensively as possible. My suggestion to you if you want to finish your testimony by the end of tomorrow's business is to be concise, to be precise to the point; in other words, to answer the whole question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Don't give more information than you are asked for because that will entail -- would invite -- will invite more questions and would probably mean that you'll be still here on Monday if not also on Tuesday. If you take my advice, you'll be out of this courtroom and of this building by the end of tomorrow quarter to 2.00 at the latest. Thank you. Mr. Cunningham, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your name is Mirko Dejanovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You and I have met before, and in our conversations yesterday and today you indicated that you wanted to testify in English. Is that the case? Or would you feel more comfortable testifying in your native language? It's really your choice.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my desire to speed up the proceedings, I am prepared to testify in English. Should there be any problems, I would like to go back to my own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. That's certainly fine with everyone here. But let me caution you even though you and I both speak English, all of your answers need to be translated into other languages, so you need to give -- we can't talk too quickly. You need to give the interpreters enough time to answer. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We need this for the record. Could you tell the Chamber your date of birth. When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born 10th of July, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The binder that you brought in, the binder that's in front of you is a book containing some exhibits that I gave to you earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. When I refer to an exhibit, I'll try to refer you to the tab number that's in there. I know you've looked at these documents. But if at any time you get a document today, if you need time to look at it, please take the time to read it so that you're comfortable with it. You told us you were born on 10 July 1963. Where were you born at?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Kostajnica. It's a little place in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you raised in Croatia? Were you raised somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, at that time. My family already lived in Bosanska Kostajnica, and I was raised in Bosanska Kostajnica in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What municipality do you currently reside in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am currently living in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, can we go into private session for about four background questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told you were raised in Bosanska Kostajnica. Did you attend secondary school there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I attended secondary school in Kostajnica in Croatia. Elementary school, I attended in Bosanska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And upon graduation from secondary school, did you attend university?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you receive a diploma?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I finished economy, school of economy at the University of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when did you receive your diploma?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was 1986, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that you were raised in the area of Bosanska Kostajnica. Is your family from that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How long have they lived in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's more than 200 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was that area of the former Yugoslavia an area that suffered casualties during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did your family suffer casualties during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the Second World War, all men with age over the 14 years had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And roughly speaking, how many people was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's, if I'm talking about my family, I'm thinking a few houses. It's 18 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did those individuals die, those men, 18 men, die in combat operations or some other way?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And briefly, how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: That happened when during the World War, there was an independent Croatian state, so-called independent Croatian state which covered Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the army of that state collected all that people, not just from my family, but also from all other families and simply shooted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Growing up where you did, did you grow up exclusively among Serbs, or did you have friends and acquaintances from the other nations, the other people?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't raise isolated. Even all these places in Bosnia had some neighbours with people from one nation. We get together at school. We play together football. We had one football club. And also some -- I had a -- I have a sister-in-law, she is a Croat. I have my best man's wife is Bosniaks and so on. It means we grow up together for a long time, for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you have relationships, friendships, with non-Serbs while you attended university?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I did. I share my bed for one year, not room, bed, with one Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After graduating from university in Banja Luka, where did you go? Did you return home?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I returned to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in 1986 or about then when you returned home, what sort of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was reason why I went back to my home, because I had a job in a factory, metal factory, in my raised place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was your position at this metal factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I started as a salesclerk. Then after that, I performed some other positions, sales manager and financial manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How long did you work at this metal factory in your home municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was about five years, maybe a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you returned to the municipality of Bosanski Novi, where did you live? What town?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to municipality, I lived in my parents' home in Kostajnica, Bosanska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is show you an exhibit. It's an exhibit that is a map of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. I believe this is Exhibit 1624. Now, I'm going to ask you to point out some areas on the map, and what you're going to have to do is not point at the screen but rather at the actual map itself. Could you point out for the Chamber, please, where your town, your village of Bosanski Kostajnica is.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's at the very top of the map with a blue dot. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And it's apparent from your earlier answer, but what is right across -- is there a river that flows through Bosanski Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: From Bosanski Novi to Bosanska Kostajnica, and far away, there is River Una, which is the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the early 1990s, what was the population of Bosanska Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's approximately 70 per cent were Serbs, and 29 per cent Muslims, and 1 per cent other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what would the population be in actual numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the city, let's say city, was 3.500 people. And in the villages around, around Kostajnica, there was another 3.000, maybe fully 6.500 people, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we were to follow the Una River south and west, would that take us down to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is there an area in the municipality, and I apologise if I mispronounce this, known as the Japra Valley?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Japra valley is - that's what I'm showing - from Donji Agici to Blagaj Japra. That's we call the Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It appears on the route that you traced that it goes through some -- there are some villages in that area. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bozici, Suhaca, Joseva, Maslovare, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What is the -- is there a sizeable Muslim population in the Japra Valley?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What is the distance as the crow flies between Bosanska Kostajnica to the Japra Valley?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, if we are talking about Blagaj Japra, it's about 40 kilometres to Kostajnica, maybe little bit less, 38 or something like that. But to Donji Agici, it's an additional, I think, 14 kilometres. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm done with the map. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the 1980s, while you were a student and after you completed your studies at Banja Luka University, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have any political activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did there come a time in the early 1990s that you became interested in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me just to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was at the time when national parties all over the Yugoslavia had been established, and in Croatia, HDZ had been established. And later on, HDZ in Bosnia had been established. And later on SDA, as parties from -- of Croats and Bosniak people -- let's say, population. Simply having in mind that what I had in my, let's say, experience listening stories from my parents, listening what happened during the Second World War in my region and having in mind my historical, let's say, knowledge, and having in mind that people in place where I was born and where I raised had really big confidence in me, it seemed to me that it is better for me to get involved in political life than to stay out of that and give some mixed extremist or some other people to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's break that down a little bit. When the national parties started forming, the HDZ, did they - specifically with the HDZ - did they use certainly national or nationalistic symbols?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is -- what was very frightening for Serbs in that time is the symbols which -- and words, words -- wording which that parties started to use, symbols, for example, flags, coat of arms, or some songs or something like that. Everything was what reminded Serbs of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We talked about the HDZ, the flags, the coat of arms, those things. What about the formation of the SDA? Did that raise any similar concerns?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They had also their own flags and coat of arms. But what especially frightened Serbs was exhibitions on the common meetings, common assemblies of that two parties, especially probably you know about tying up together flags and all other expressions which they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, you are a well-educated man, an intelligent man. Why did that cause fear in you and other people in the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe it looks different from the point of view from this time, and I know very well that from the foreigners from the Westerns, it seems very unreasonable that the symbols could produce some fear in -- to one people. But the situation in which we were, fresh remembers of the World War II, and combined with those symbols and combined with political activities which led to separation and secession of former Yugoslavia, that is something that really frightened not only ordinary people, but also little bit more educated people or intellectuals or everybody else. It is something that is connected with our history which we know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about the SDS in Bosanski Novi. Were you approached to become a candidate or to join the party?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was asked, let's say, from local people who knew me very well. I was strongly asked to join the SDS party for all the reason I already said. And I decided to join the party. Immediately after I decided that, I was appointed to be president of local SDS in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when did that appointment happen?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. In 1991. I can't remember exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's okay. Did you ultimately get appointed to another position within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not ultimately. That was, let's say, political procedure. Later on, I was appointed to be member of local parliament. And later on I was appointed to be president of Bosanski Novi committee of SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So you were a member of the -- I guess the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Municipal assembly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And when you say "president of the Bosanski Novi committee of the SDS," is that also known as the SDS main board?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, SDS main board.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What qualified you to serve in that position? How is it that you got that position?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was elected between some people. I suppose it was probably my education because not a lot of people in that time had a university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us in -- at university, you told us while you were at the metal factory -- I didn't ask you this, so let me back up. While you were working at the metal factory, were there non-Serbs working at that factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what sort of reputation did you enjoy or have with the non-Serb workers ter factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe I had great respect, and I believe I still have quite a big respect from non-Serb population in my born place. Mostly of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Novi. You were a member of the assembly. After the multiparty elections, who had the majority in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: SDS had the majority. The second party was SDA, and there were two smaller parties, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember the breakdown in seats; that is, how many seats the SDS had, how many seats the SDA had, and then the two minor parties? And if you can't remember the exact numbers, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me see. It was maybe 36 SDS, maybe 17 SDA, and then both minor parties had 5 seats. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were there any SDA members of the executive council of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Generally speaking, after the multiparty elections, how did things work in the municipal assembly? Did the parties get along? Describe that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Even already there were some disputes in a former country. I think I can say that we worked quite normal and quite correct between our parties. You know, it's when you elect local assembly, then you have to fulfill some executive committee and to solve some personal issues, and then all other issues. I think we worked correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. Did there come a time when the SDA members walked out of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember the exact date? And if you can't remember the exact date, do you happen to recall the event that prompted their walkout of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember exact date. But I remember very well what was the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We tried, and we had interest, SDS representatives, to join to ZOBK - I'm not sure I can translate it, I hope you understand what I'm talking about - and later that was called ARK. Bosniak representatives didn't want to adopt that decision. Later on, we adopted that decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there because we'll talk about the ARK later. So you don't need to go into that right now.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That was the reason for leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there a similar walkout of the SDA members that were on the executive council?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not only executive council, and also from some other positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were the SDA members replaced in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When we say --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you remember how much later -- how much down the road they were replaced? Was it weeks? Months? Years?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it's weeks, but not months, not days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were the SDA members replaced on the executive council?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The replacements, which ethnicities were they of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk to you about the war in Croatia. In 1991, when the war in Croatia started, did that have an impact on your municipality of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that had great impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We -- on the map earlier, we showed that your -- the place where you were raised, Bosanski Kostajnica is right across the Una River from Croatia. In your municipality were there actual war operations, combat operations during the war with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that time, Croatian army and police tried to get control over the Kostajnica and all other places around there. And that caused some battles and combats and so on. JNA in that time was official -- still official army of the former country. And JNA was involved on some level in that conflict. Of course, that caused a lot of problems including some deaths and a lot of refugees and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Because of Bosanski Novi's proximity, it's closeness to Croatia, was it common or uncommon to see JNA men, equipment, going through your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bosanski Novi is a very frequent place where you can go to a lot of other places. And it was very usual to see a lot of army going through the Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the war affect the commercial relations, the economy of the municipality of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say extremely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Former country Yugoslavia was one market, let's say, of 20 million people. And especially Bosnia and Herzegovina's companies had production which -- and they sell their products all over Yugoslavia. Starting with break of Yugoslavia caused a lot of problems, especially we couldn't sell our products. But also, some supplying systems, some electricity system and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With the impact on your markets because you said you couldn't sell your products and the impact of your supply systems, how did that affect the employment? Did the level of jobs remain the same? Increase? Or decrease?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The employment decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did people lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was it only Bosniaks, Muslims, who lost jobs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have exact figures, but a lot of people stopped to work because simply companies couldn't work, not only Bosniaks, but if companies stopped to work, normally work stops Bosniaks and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During 1991 with the conflict in Croatia, were there call-ups? Were there mobilisations of conscripts from the local community?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That was a lawyer question. Let me break it down into real English. Were there call-ups during the conflict in Croatia? Were people being called into the service?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Mobilisation has been started.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was the -- in your municipality, what was the attitude, the response of the Muslim population to the mobilisation? Did they respond or not respond?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Some Muslims respond to the mobilisation, especially in the first stage. But later on, not. A majority of Muslims didn't respond to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the law of the former Yugoslavia, if an individual did not respond to mobilisation, could there be consequences? Could it affect that person's employment?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, they could be fired. They should be fired. According to law, if they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in Bosanski Novi, if an individual did not respond to mobilisation, what would happen to his employment?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I remember, they were not fired automatically. Simply we were waiting for some political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did that political solution ever come about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, with Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. But certainly not in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What if a -- based on your knowledge of Bosanski Novi in 1991, 1992 -- let's just stick with 1991. If a Serb did not respond to mobilisation, what consequences did he face?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: He should be also fired, or he should be also treated equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And did that happen? When I say "that," were Serbs and non-Serbs treated equally if they failed to respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe in that time that we still -- we treated people equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With the presence of military equipment in the JNA in your municipality and the war across the river, were there any restrictions placed on civilians moving within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no official restrictions in terms of freedom of movement. Of course, the war was close to people's home, just across the river. And nobody feel happy to travel, for example, through the night or...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your answer -- you said in your answer that there were no official restrictions. What do you mean when you say "no official restrictions"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no curfew. There was no prohibition for any group or any individuals to move freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I ask, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, if we could get a period of time, as Mr. Ackerman kept asking me. At the moment I'm not sure what period were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're a hundred per cent right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When in 1991 did war operations, combat operations come to the vicinity, come to near?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was summer of 1991. I can't, again, remember exact dates. But it was July, August, maybe September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. So let's talk about the period of time before July, August of 1991. As far as you know, were there any restrictions on movement within the --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At this time period, in 1991, where were you working? Were you working in Kostajnica or in Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that time, I think I worked in Kostajnica. In that time in Kostajnica, but later on I moved my job to Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that the war operations started July, August. During that time period, were there any curfews imposed by the civil authorities to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not official curfews, or not curfews at all. But there was some fear to travel during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With the presence of the military in the community, were there any checkpoints or barricades set up during the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When do you remember, roughly speaking, approximate when the hostilities ended in your -- in the vicinity of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It ended -- you are talking about war connected with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It ended, I think -- as I said, in September, I think. Maybe later August or early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And at the end of the war in August or early September 1991, were you still working in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was your job there? Were you still at the metal factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, at that time I was financial manager in that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, did the -- at the termination in September, August, September 1991, did the economy bounce back?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not off. The economy was still very weak, and we still didn't solve the problem -- economy problems I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, do you remember whether the SDA left the municipal assembly before or after August, September 1991, the end of the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's after that. Quite a long -- quite a long period after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you told us earlier that had to do because they did not agree, the SDA did not agree, with the SDS position with respect to the ZOBK. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: As a member of the municipal assembly and a member of the SDS main -- municipal main board, did you have an interest in the ZOBK? Was it something that appealed first to you, and then secondly to the party?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It simply appeared. Before that there was a solution in former Yugoslavia constitution to join some municipalities in some association. In that period, period of big crisis, it appeared -- ZOBK appeared as a possible solution to solve some economic issues, some infrastructure issues. But later on as the political issues rise in all country, it also appeared as a solution for solving political problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let's break down your answer and talk about how it appealled -- excuse me, appeared as a possible solution to some economic issues, some infrastructure issues. What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about electricity system, about telephone system, about railway system, about payment system, financial banking system and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How would the ZOBK, how would this entity assist in the infrastructure and the economic issues?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's say if we are talking about electricity, you know, the electricity system has to be a system. You can't have your own electricity in one municipal. You have to have enough big space if you want to organise electricity supplying system. As already problems started in -- with Bosnian government started with activities to secede from Yugoslavia, that also impact on electricity supplying system. I can say, for example, that we had had to sit and to agree. For example, we could have only two or three hundred kilowatts of electricity, our municipality. And then we have to discuss about how much which municipality should have electricity to enable some companies to work. That was, for example, one question. I can point to some other examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I appreciate that. But let's try to get back on track a little bit. Was the ZOBK -- and let me back up. When the ZOBK was first proposed, did you and your colleagues within the party look at this statute or the proposed statute of the ZOBK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I understand. Yes, we look at it and recognise it is a good solution for our municipality also.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was it mandatory that Novi join?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it was mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But Novi didn't join the ZOBK, did it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We needed two-thirds of a vote to join the ZOBK according to statute of the municipality. In that time, we couldn't reach that volume of votes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two-thirds of what? The majority of which votes? Of whose votes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Local assembly. Local assembly had 70 seats, and we needed two-thirds of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So did the problem arise because the SDS -- SDA members walked out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The SDA members were still there. The problem is because they didn't want to vote for that, and some other -- from minority parties, some members didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had 36 votes there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many votes did you have? How many seats did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We needed just one vote more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one more, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I asked you if it was mandatory for Novi to join, and I think you might have misunderstood me. When I said "mandatory," was it --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's okay. Please don't worry about it. Did every municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they required to join?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we were not required. Now, I understand. It was a mistake. We have to decide on our own whether we would like or not to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you originally examined the statute, what was your primary motivation? Was it economic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was economic. And when I'm talking about economic, I'm firstly thinking infrastructure issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that the SDA did not agree that the municipality should join the ZOBK. You didn't get the required two-thirds vote. Ultimately, did your municipality join an association known as the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was our -- in the meantime, the association changed its name. And we in a third attempt, we succeeded to have enough votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you got to two-thirds vote.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: From the municipal assembly and joined. Do you happen to know when you got the two-thirds vote?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We got --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's my fault because it wasn't a clear question. Do you remember the date where you joined the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really remember the date. But I know that it is after all other municipalities formed and joined to the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Was the ARK intended -- was the ARK a level of government?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is association, not -- it can't be government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want you to look at I think -- look in your notebook in front of you. It should be tab number 2, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 61. And this is in evidence, and it is a list of the representatives in the Krajina Autonomous Region Assembly. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I see my name. It's number 93, but it is connected with the wrong municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know how that happened, or is that just -- obviously that's a typographical error. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's very obviously, because Bosanski Novi is immediately after that. After my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There is you, and one, two, three --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: -- Four other people --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Me and other three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're right. It appears to me that some of these other municipalities have six or seven members. Why is it that it appears that Novi had four?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: All other municipalities had seven, let's say, seats. We appointed just the four, four representatives to Assembly for AR Krajina willing to keep three other seats to Bosniak people because we believed that they will also join, they will change their mind, they will appoint their representatives for assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was it intended that the ARK be a -- solely a Serb entity?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not intended, and especially in our case, in Novi grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why did you feel it was appropriate especially in Novi to have the SDA, the Muslims, involved in this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me say that just some other municipalities had some Bosniak or non-Serb representatives. And we believe that this is a good solution for all of us, and also we believed that it is solution to get together, to get together in solving all the problems which I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in talking about the problems of the future of Yugoslavia. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you are talking about political problems. But also about economical and infrastructural problems, that was the way we could solve all that problems together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your notebook, I would like you to go to tab 4, which is Exhibit 2354, and that is the statute -- I'm sorry. I've got the wrong exhibit. You told us this is the statute of the ZOBK. You told us that obviously that became the ARK. During your time as a member of the municipal assembly, as a member of the ARK Assembly, as a member of the SDS main board, did you have the opportunity to read the statute that in effect set up the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because we were discussing about that local assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What was necessary before a decision of the ARK Assembly? What was needed before a decision on the ARK Assembly -- decision of the ARK Assembly would be binding upon the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was necessary that that decision also has to be also adopted in local assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that you were appointed to become a member of the ARK Assembly. Were you aware of ever any elections to select representatives to the ARK Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not. It was -- we were delegated. We say that, from the local municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the ARK have executive powers over the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How about legislative powers over the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings of the ARK Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Several of them. Or let's say, just a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you say "a few," how many are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Two or maybe three. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where were the meetings held at?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Specifically where in Banja Luka were they held at?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was -- We call that building Banski Dvor, it's in the centre of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where inside Banski Dvor were the assembly meetings held at?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two halls, two rooms. I think we met in both, but I'm not sure. There were bigger and smaller rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What were the meetings like? Could you describe for the Chamber the atmosphere of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: For me - and that was why we were there just two or three times - it was like Hyde Park. Everyone could enter. Everyone can have a speech. Everyone can go out whenever he wants and so on. It was very unserious job. It was really funny, let's say, because there is no minutes, there is no rules about proceeding these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to come to that conclusion that it was not serious?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say in days or months. But it was after two or three meetings. I realise that it is really unserious job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And as a result of your conclusion that it's not -- what was your perception of the ARK Assembly's power or its competence?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You know, competent can have two meanings. It can deal with a person's ability or lack of ability, or the powers of the -- that the entity has, so let's take it --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think both missing in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was the reaction when you had returned to Novi as a member of the ARK Assembly? How did the people in Novi react to the ARK Assembly? I don't know if that makes any sense.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we come back from that meeting, of course we have to -- we had to discuss, we had to inform all other peoples what's going on, how it is going on. What we said, me and my friends in the assembly, what we had to local assembly, to local people was that definitely we should care about ourselves on our own. That was my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Expand upon that a little bit because that's not clear to me. Did you think -- what prompted you to say that? I don't want to ask you a leading question that might suggest an answer. But explain a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply, we still wanted and we still believed that we should find some solutions for all problems I was talking about. But when you are coming to Banja Luka and see how it is going on, we were coming back to Novi Grad or Bosanski Novi and sit around and discuss that. And I told to all other people that we should think a lot more about ourselves because we can't expect that that body or that association could help us. We didn't leave that association because we still believed that it will improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there hope that the ARK could be a vehicle to resolve the political issues?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Because, you know, regional approach, let's say, was already very interesting thing in all Europe, and we believed that through regional approach, through regional organisations and through regional cooperation, we could solve all that problems in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about a document that's in the book. It's Document P25. And that's tab number -- actually, it's apparently not in your book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise to the usher. I'll need your help in showing the exhibit, P25, to the witness, please. I'm sorry, I made a mistake. It's number 8. If you could look at number 8. It's tab number 8 in his book. I apologise, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This document dated 19 December 1991 is entitled: "Instructions for the organisation and activity of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances." Did you ever see this document in 1991 or in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: You showed me this document when we first time talked. Before that, I've never seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the first time we talked was a month, month and a half ago, something --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So you never saw this in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw it and I never dealt with that. And I read it and I think it's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why do you think it's ridiculous?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Because if we are reading some variants, and if we are comparing this variant A, which what should be in the case of Bosanski Novi, simply it was not like that. Nothing happened like that, or main things didn't happen like that, like it is wrote there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Go to the next tab, which is Exhibit 157, Tab 9, this is a document, an excerpt, entitled: "From instructions for the work of the municipal crisis staffs of the Serbian people." It's dated 26 April 1992, attributed to Branko Dzeric, Prime Minister. Did you see that document in 1992 as an SDS member of the municipal assembly and member of the SDS main board in Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I see this document and I know about it. But I see it by virtue of my position and especially by virtue that I was from Bosanska Kostajnica, which is quite, let's say, separated area in Bosanski Novi and by virtue that I'm coming from that, I was involved in some later activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you a -- This document talks about crisis staffs. By virtue of your position as president of the local main board, were you a member of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that I think in that time, I was already a member of main board in Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I attended to some meetings of crisis staff in Novi Grad, even we didn't have a lot of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So let me make sure I understand. There was obviously a crisis staff in Novi Grad. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you were a member of that crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk about specific events in 1992, the spring and early summer of 1992. And first of all, I want to talk with you about the police department in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. In the spring of 1992, were there Muslim policemen, Bosniak policemen, on the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did something happen that caused some of the Muslim police to leave their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that time, police changed the signs on the uniforms. And I think uniforms also. That caused the -- that some Bosniak police didn't want to accept that signs and uniforms, and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Muslim, the Bosniak police officers were also required to take some sort of loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did some non-Serbs including Bosniaks remain on the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I know about Kostajnica, that for sure some non-Serbs, both Bosniaks and Croats, were still in the police after that. I'm not sure for police station in Bosanski Novi. Maybe yes; maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. How many officers, how many policemen would there be typically in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It used to be between the Second World War and the early 1990s, usually it was always six policemens. But I think in early 1990s, various number, just for a few of them. And there was already a reserve policemens who were started to work every day. I'm talking both about reserve police and active police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Right. I guess what I'm trying to have you answer is how many non-Serbs were there on the local force in Kostajnica and how many of them remained?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately ten of them professionally. I'm talking about professional police. And I'm sure that two of Bosniaks which worked there remained, both of them. They worked and they remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you right there. Does that mean there was a total of ten officers on the force, and then two --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: About ten. And then we have reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how many --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: And there were some Croats in the reserve police, I know for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How many of them remained in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the two of them, the Croats, were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you have a good relationship with the local SDA and the local Muslims police officers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What sort of relationship did you have with the chief of police or -- in Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of police in Novi, I know him very well. He's my friend. He was my friend at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What about the police station in Kostajnica, who was the head of that police station?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: One man, Sucur [phoen] is his surname. He's also my friend. He was chief of that small department.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're going to take a break at about quarter to, this is an excellent stopping point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. We will have a break, and we will reconvene as early as possible dealing with the Maglov case. And then we will proceed. We are going to have a break now during which I hope you will be served coffee and you can have a little rest. It will be roughly in about an hour's time that you will be called again because in the meantime we are dealing with another short case, another matter in which, of course, you are not involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll reconvene in about 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bring Mr. Brdjanin in, and then we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, one of the things I want to do is I want to clear up a mistake that I made in my terminology. Earlier you told us that you were a member of the SDS board in Novi, and I refer to that as the main board. In reality, that's called the municipal board. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's main board for municipal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were on the board in Kostajnica, technically speaking, that's the board for the commune of Kostajnica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I wanted to clear that up. If you could, we'll get back on track and go back to talking about the events in the spring and early summer of 1992. And if you could, in the binder in front of you, go to tab number 10. Tab number 10 is Prosecutor's Exhibit 227 which is the Official Gazette of the ARK. The very first decision, the one that should be in front of you right now, is a decision pursuant to the decision of the Ministry of Defence. It is a document dated 4 May 1992 from the secretary of the National Defence Secretariat of the ARK, Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic. Number 5, notation in this decision says: "All paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally possess weapons and ammunition are to immediately, and by 1500 hours on 11 May 1992 at the latest, surrender them." And we can see the rest of the document there. I want to talk to you about this: In May, the first part of May 1992, what part of the municipality were you spending the bulk of your time in? Were you all over the municipality, or in one -- spending most of your time in one portion of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was working in Novi Grad, and some of my duties related to my job, I performed in Novi Grad. But usually I spent the time in Kostajnica because it was already tough time, and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You say it was a tough time. Let's -- if you could, describe for the Chamber what made it a tough time, say, at the end of April, early May of 1992? Were tensions increasing in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tensions increasing, especially related what started in Sarajevo and all over the Bosnia and the referendum of the plebiscite. And then some events in Slavonski Brod, and then tensions rised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was -- were there concerns among the population about other peoples having weapons? Were the Serbs concerned about the Muslims have been weapons and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were both, both concerns very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This decision in Exhibit P227, the one that I read out, were you aware of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I'm aware very well because I'm -- I was not very close to, let's say, military issues, but I don't know. Probably it was issued. Even we had a Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that time, and there was Ministry of Defence because I'm not sure this gentleman was authorised to issue this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm not really -- at this stage, I'm not really concerned about whether or not he's authorised. What I'm concerned about is the subject matter of paragraph 5, which has to deal with paramilitary formations, the possession of weapons, illegal weapons, and ammunition, and the surrendering of them. In late April, early May of 1992, what steps, if any, did you take to deal with the rising tensions that you just described?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was really trying to deal both with Bosniaks and with Serbs, trying to calm down the situation and to keep peace, let's say. I was permanently trying to be in contact with all sides because of all these concerns about weapons, and I tried simply to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, what area of the municipality, what region of the municipality did you have any influence in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had influence in my, let's say, born place. When I'm saying "born place," I'm thinking about Bosanska Kostajnica. I had influence in that area. Because of that, I spent a lot of time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay, now, you said that you were permanently trying to be in contact with all sides, trying to calm down the situation. In this respect, what did you do? First of all, did you do anything to -- were you working with the SDA and the Muslims in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, among other things I've done, I went to the mosque, talked to Islam priest, hodza, we call that, that you say usually hodza is the most influenced man among Muslim people. I went to the mosque, stayed there for a long time. Not only me, me and local Orthodox priest, we went to the mosque, talked to people. We tried to find a solution how to calm down situation, how the Muslims could express, let's say, good faith. And we settled one agreement, let's say, that Bosniak should collect any possible weapon they have, and then we -- they collect some weapons, some real weapons and some handmade weapons which they had, and we -- they put it on the bags. And publicly, came to the police station and surrendered their weapons. That enabled me to go to the Serbian population and say, "okay, Bosniaks, they surrendered their weapons. They're not any dangerous for us. Let's keep calm down. We can deal with that problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You talked how you -- by the way, are we talking about -- your efforts, are these -- what time of the year? Is it April, May? Give us a time frame.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was around - I'm not sure - 11th or 10 May, something like these days. At the time of the matter of the collecting weapons or surrendering weapons from the paramilitary and other groups was on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you're working with -- and we're going to talk about what, if anything, with the Serbian population. But in your dealings with the Muslim population, was that simply on one day? Was it just this one meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it lasts for days. The other days I -- of course, there was need to encourage local Muslim population. Then I done that with just walking through the streets during the early night, about 9.00 or 10.00, meeting people, talking to them and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how could that, just walking through the streets and meeting people and talking to them, how could that have any effect? Did that have to do with who you were and your reputation there? Describe that for us.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they believed me in that time, and I was really open and honest to them. And I think a lot of people -- let's say all the people knew me, both Bosniaks and Serbs. They knew me. I grew up in that place. My father was there. One part of our life, we used to live in the society where the Bosniaks lived. Simply I think they believed me. I talked to them, "let's keep calm down, I hope everything will be solved," and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us about what you were doing on the Muslim side of the situation, and that included convincing them to turn in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think turning weapons from the Bosniaks was very important because even if they have or if they have not weapons, it didn't mean nothing because they were minority. But they could do great thing if they surrender any weapons as a good faith, let's say. And because of that, I asked them, I asked both sides to surrender weapons. But from other reasons. I'd like also the Serbs' paramilitary forces to be disarmed, and I called them also to surrender the weapons. And from the Bosniak side, I asked them to surrender weapons in order to find some signal of good faith which could enable us, let's say, politicians, local politicians, to have some instrument to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to follow up on something that you said there. You said: "I'd like also that the Serbs' paramilitary forces to be disarmed, and I called them also to surrender their weapons." Now I'd like you to tell us what you did with respect to the Serbian population to get them to surrender their weapons. Because I take it, did the Muslim population ever tell you: "We are frightened of the Serbs"? Was there fear on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was fear on both sides, and there was fear also -- there was fear about paramilitary units on both sides, same. What I tried to do is in constant contact with the police chief, we also always asking for paramilitary groups and for criminals to be disarmed or to be put in the control. I can give you one example. It's maybe -- I have no right probably for closed session, but there was one --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. Is there an individual's name --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There's individuals --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I mean, with the Court's permission, if we could go into closed session -- private session?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Private, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any problems, Ms. Korner? Not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies. Let's go into private session for a while. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Let's proceed, Mr. Cunningham. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want you to describe in detail what you did first with respect to the Serbian paramilitaries in an effort to disarm them. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I was not authorised to take any actions, military or police actions. But what I could do is politically to put always that problem on the table and discuss about that and ask all governmental levels or institutions to deal with that and to disarm that. That was only what I could do, and I've done that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that the head of the police in Kostajnica was someone that you had a good working relationship with. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Both in Kostajnica and in Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You made your requests upon these police officers; did they take any action? Was there an effort made to - let me finish - was there an effort made to disarm Serbian paramilitaries that may have been on the territory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we tried that. I already told about one, let's say, the biggest problem. But I believe they tried always to disarm the -- even they were also not capable for big deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you say that "they were not capable for a big deal," I think I know what you're talking about, but it's not really clear for the record. So explain that a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My fault. Are you talking about the capability of the local police or what?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about capability of local police because it was chaotic situation, and there was a lot of, let's say, paramilitary groups or the group. The war was just across the river. A lot of people had relatives, friends across the river in Croatia. And a lot of people from the Bosnian side, as volunteers, took part in the war in Croatia. That was one thing. That people sometimes came with arms to the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there because we're talking about May of 1992. Was that still a recurring problem in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain the situation that that produced a lot of groups and a lot of arms all around. Also, the war in that time, there was still war in the Croatia, but it was not on the River Una. It was, let's say, 30 or 40 kilometres far away. There was still war. There were a lot of groups from -- I don't know. From everywhere. And that's what I thought when I tell that the local police was not capable to deal with all these groups and individuals and so on. Because again, Novi was very, very specifically situated, and it was cross point for a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were those groups -- I take it then from your answer that those groups, some of those groups, at least, were still in the municipality. On the territory of the municipality in April and May of 1992? Were they still a problem then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, they were a -- we felt they were a problem. They will be a problem, that groups. Even still, if we are talking about April, May, still, there was no any, let's say, actions. But we knew that the problem with that groups will arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Earlier in describing the Muslims, you talked about how they made a -- in good faith, they turned over some weapons. Did the police in Novi, using your term, did they in your opinion make a good-faith effort to deal with these paramilitaries to get their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm talking about Serbs, and I'm specifically talking about April and, more importantly, May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Again, I think they had good faith, but they were not capable enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We've talked about the efforts to deal with Serbian paramilitaries. Were there just regular Serbian citizens who had weapons during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was still time when we recognised JNA as the official army of Yugoslavia and official army on that territory. There was also a TO, which is subordinated to JNA, which we also recognised as official military units. They were fulfilled mostly with Serbs. Even, again, in Kostajnica, we had some Muslims involved in that units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not answering your question. Perhaps he may have misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I was going to rephrase it, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, okay. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It was my fault because I referred to Serbian citizens with weapons. And what I'm really getting at is Serbian civilians, not affiliated with the TO, not affiliated with the JNA, just a regular civilian who had weapons. Were these -- you talked about how you approached the Muslims on weapons; you've talked about the Serbian paramilitaries. Tell us what if any efforts you personally took to convince the Serbian -- the regular Serbian civilian who had a weapon to put that weapon up or turn it in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no -- there was no need for Serbian civilian to be armed. There was TO, there was JNA. There was mobilisation that -- if anyone received invitation for mobilisation, he could go to the army. There was simply no need, and I'm not aware about any armed civilians, if I'm clear now, because the Serbs responded to the mobilisation. There was no need for some civilians to be armed. If they are armed out of the JNA or TO, it is paramilitary group simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever approach any individual Serbian citizens who were not affiliated with the TO, not with the JNA, to turn in their hunting rifles, their licensed pistols? Did you make a similar request on the Serbian civilian population that you made to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
