utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What part of the municipality was your focus in in trying to reduce these tensions? Was it Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, it was Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you believe that your efforts bore any fruit? Were they successful?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in that critical period, we didn't have any victims, any -- we didn't have any combat between Serbs and -- I think from the point of view in that time, that was great success comparing with what happened in all other...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You use a phrase in your answer: "We didn't have any victims." I want to talk to you, and I want you to remember what you said there because I want you to talk about whether or not there were any problems with either paramilitaries or parapolice coming to Kostajnica. First of all, did they come to Kostajnica, the parapolice?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They come a little bit later. I'm not sure. It was the end of May, I think, came one group to Kostajnica, which caused a lot of problems in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, please, when I told victim, I was thinking about murdered people, not about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could both speakers please kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't know if you heard the interpreter, but we're going a little bit too fast. So we need to slow down, and let's remember that everything is being translated.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that at the end of May, you believe a group came to Kostajnica which caused a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was this a group of police? Or parapolice?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as police. By what they've done later on, I think it's a criminal group. I don't believe it's real police. But still, we don't know them -- any one of them because they were not from local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You say "by what they've done later." What did they do to the citizens, specifically the Muslim citizens of Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They beat them, robbed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not immediately, because, you know, I was travelling and going up and down. And one day when I back home, some Serbs, local Serbs, told me that it is something unusual and terrified what that people are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Did you investigate it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I contacted police officers, and they confirmed me that it's a group which is -- which are not doing like police. They are doing like robbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that you had a good working relationship with the head of the police in Kostajnica. Did you and he do anything to try to resolve this problem and to deal with the parapolice and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I strongly asked him to take some step in order to -- for that people to leave the territory. And also, we let's say send them the message if they don't leave, we will try to self-organise and beat against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And let's take it first step. What did the -- specifically, what did the head of the police in Kostajnica do to get these people to stop? What's the first step? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: He's done only what he could to done. He phoned police chief, and they send some letter, I don't know where, telling that that group is a problem and the Serbs are very, let's say, afraid what they are doing. They are not accepting that. And it will be a problem if they don't leave as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there ever a confrontation between you and other Serbs that were opposed to this sort of behaviour in the parapolice?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: One of that guy from that so-called police units, probably knowing what happened, he tried to threaten me. He threaten me that I will be arrested, I am -- I am trying to stop them to do their job, I'm protecting Muslims and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what ultimately happened with this group of parapolice?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, I don't know how long a time, but not so long time after that, they left Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you know why they left?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They left.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Muslim population in Kostajnica when they left?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: After all, they were frightened, of course. But I believe it was much easier for them. They were happy when that group left, even -- they already made quite a lot of bad things. And they stayed, I think, a little bit frightened after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did a -- did any of the Muslim population of Kostajnica leave because of this fear? Did they move away because of this fear you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe some of them, yes. Even from Kostajnica, we never had, let's say, big group or convoy or something like that, people leaving Kostajnica. I don't know exact number, but big number of Muslims stayed in Kostajnica during all the time of war. But some of them left later on during the war, one by one, but also a lot of Serbs left also because of economic situation and because of fear they felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you feel that your efforts in Kostajnica were effective in reducing the tensions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is, after all, after the war, I'm meeting that people, I'm sitting with them in cafes and discussing. Even with some guys which was under the, let's say, torture of this group in that time. They never tell me anything wrong about my role in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you're referring to these people, you're referring to which population? Bosniak population?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bosniak population, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, we've talked about your efforts in the northeast or the northern part of the municipality. I want to talk about events in other parts of the municipality. Earlier in your examination, you pointed out to us on the map where the Japra Valley was. In early May, in April and May, were the same sort of tensions in that part of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you try to go to the Japra Valley to -- as you did in Kostajnica, to try to reduce the tension there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything happened in quite a short period of time. I did not have time to left the situation in Kostajnica and go to other places. Some other people tried to calm down the situation there, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was -- the situation, was this a concern of the local SDS municipal board or the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it concerned us. We were discussed about that. On several occasions, we tried to persuade people publicly, on the meetings, that we should calm down the situation. We should stop all bad things what started, if we can. But again, it was on the meetings where we discussed what was going on, we were concerned about the situation in Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why were you concerned about the situation there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exact date, but the problems appeared there. I'm informed that paramilitary groups made some attack on military police. And I don't know about that even then. I'm not sure where that happened and when exactly. But that was -- that caused, let's say, a lot of problems between people in that area. Mostly populated by Muslims and with some villages with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was -- like someone -- like, you tried to ease the tensions in Kostajnica. Was anyone from the SDS trying to do the same thing in the Japra Valley?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were obliged. All the local SDS officials, they were obliged by our decisions to try to calm down the situation, same as we done in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were they successful like you were in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say they were because of what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let's talk about what happened there. Did you become aware, through conversations, about a large convoy of Muslims leaving the area because they were afraid --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's really horribly leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Then I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would like to know without being told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You talked about specifically the problems -- again I apologise for my pronunciation -- there was one town, Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's Japra Valley. We used to say Blagaj Japra is the same, because Blagaj and River Japra for the same. It's same thing, Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you become aware of a large group of Muslims leaving that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How did you become aware?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply, I'm informed. I can't remember who, from but I'm informed that there is a big group who wanted to leave that area. And of course, that happened after some fights, some --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Why were they wanting to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was some shelling and some shooting in that area. They were frightened. They felt great fear. And they simply wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're saying shelling and shooting. Perhaps you can be more precise on who was doing the shelling and the shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that were paramilitary forces. For me, that were paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Paramilitaries were also capable of shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say shelling, I think about, let's say, big guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking you to be clear because for me using shelling and shooting may have different connotations from what perhaps you mean to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's my misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I put the question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't know if you've answered His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't actually. He hasn't explained what he means by shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shooting by paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I still don't think you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you distinguish shooting from shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I know what you told me. Shelling should be made by big, big guns or cannons. And shooting is from, let's say, guns, small guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before these Bosniaks decided to leave the area because they were frightened as you said from shelling and shooting, was there shelling and shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was shooting, as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there was no shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Absolutely no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How many people, if you know, were trying to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only imagine that it could be five to seven thousand people. Having in mind the Bosniak population in Novi Grad. I'm not sure, but it is about maybe 5.000. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Where were they trying to go when they were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They tried, let's say, they asked to be sent to Central Bosnia. It's towards Doboj, Zenica, Sarajevo route because that area was populated mostly by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what happened with their request to be taken to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in that. I'm talking what I heard. There was a train organised for that people, and they were put on the train and went towards Doboj. Local authorities in Doboj didn't want to allow for men in our age, let's say, military age, to go to Central Bosnia because they were, as they said, afraid that people will be mobilised and turned to the people in Doboj, Serb people in Doboj. And then as I informed again, they were, let's say, separated. Women and children could go further, and mens were turned back to Novi Grad, Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What happened to the men, if you know, once they turned to Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It had to be find some solution where they could stay, and they were put on the stadium, local stadium in Novi, Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was that your idea to have them put in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not my idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who decided that they should go to the stadium, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who exactly in that period. Someone who dealt with them. I think there were some people who dealt with them directly with the Bosniaks, and they wanted to be somewhere together. And there was only, I don't know. It was the only possible solution to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. How long were they in that stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exact, but it lasted, let's say, for tens of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: For tens of days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. 20 or 30 days maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I just didn't understand your answer. Now, while they're in the stadium, you told us that you were on the municipal board and also on the crisis staff. Are there discussions on either the board or in the crisis staff on finding a solution for these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was discussion, of course. Even I can't remember did we have crisis staff at that time? We had discussions, and we asked local assembly and all local institutions for some steps. I can't remember exactly for what, but for some steps which will enable as normal life for that people as it could be in that circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, let's back up. Let's talk about ultimately did these people leave the stadium? Did they leave the stadium and leave Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They went to -- through Croatia -- to Croatia, through the region which was under the control of UNPROFOR in that time. And that was done together with -- in coordination with UNPROFOR and International Red Cross and so on. There were big negotiations about how that people could go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. Were you involved in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know based on your conversations that you had with other people in the municipality why it took so long for the arrangements to be resolved?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was, as I am told from the president of assembly, there was a resistance from both UNPROFOR and International Red Cross to take part in all organisation. And the local Serbs didn't want to do that without such kind of assistance. And it was necessary to make some preparation. You know, you must find the vehicles, you must enable that people can go with their properties as they can bring, not to be robbed at the end of the story and so on. That was why it takes a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Who was the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality was Mr. Pasic Radomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was he involved in the negotiations with the Red Cross and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was involved, as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What property did these people leave with?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They leave everything they could have with them. It means, cars and other vehicles and everything what they can put -- excuse me. We should make distance between people from the stadium and all other people who were in convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that people on stadium, they didn't have any property any more in their hands. But together with them in convoy, some other people which were not in the stadium, they joined them in that convoy. Of course, it has been tried to enable them to take their property as much as they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You've talked about moveable property. I would --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did many of these people own houses and farms and other real estate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What happened to that property?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, that was the chaos. Some people tried to use that situation to take over property from the Muslims, some Serb people, and they asked them for some kind of contract or some kind of giving them free of charge their property and so on. And they submitted -- there were different cases. Someone just left their homes. Someone gave keys to maybe their friends or some people who forced them to give them. There were different, various things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did -- were there Serbs within the municipality that felt that these transactions were -- they would be forced to give up their property, did they feel these transactions were fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of people who thought that was not fair, the transactions, or majority. We have discussed that also in the SDS. And following that, the local institutions took some steps, made some decisions or orders - I can't remember exactly what - saying that their contracts are not legal, are not made freely, are not legal, and couldn't be legal any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let's -- when you say the local institutions took some steps, specifically what did -- who were the local institutions and what were the steps that they took to prevent these sorts of transfers from going through?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was local executive board which was in charge to adopt some decisions in order to, let's say, stop all the procedure about these contracts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was that decision ever adopted by the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was confirmed by municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that when you looked at an exhibit earlier, which was the document from Prime Minister Dzeric, I think it's in April of 1992, dealing with crisis staffs, that you were on the crisis staff. Do you remember how many meetings the crisis staff of the Municipality of Bosanski Novi might have had?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but we didn't have a lot of sessions of crisis staff as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At the meetings of the crisis staff -- the municipal crisis staff, did the subject of the ARK Crisis Staff ever come up?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In front of you in tab number 10 is the Prosecutor's Exhibit 227, which is the Official Gazette of the ARK. Did you ever attend a meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you aware of anyone from Novi attending any meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware. I think nobody attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember now, almost 11 and a half years later, whether or not you received any of the decisions of the Official Gazette of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was looking at that Official Gazette, and really I can't remember that I read it at that time and that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I left a copy of P227 with you overnight to see if you -- to give you the opportunity to read it, to study it. Looking back now after the fact, do you remember getting any of these decisions that are contained within P227?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that we dealt with any of these things in that time. We had a lot of things, a lot of problems on the ground. I think we haven't dealt with these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During 1992, specifically during the period of May through July of 1992, you, as a member of the municipal assembly, a member of the municipal crisis staff, did you believe that you were required to implement the decisions, conclusions of the ARK crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when I'm reading these decisions, I can say that we simply didn't or I simply didn't do a lot of -- I didn't do anything from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand that you said you didn't do anything, but I want to know if the municipal crisis staff did anything with respect to these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I remember, we didn't even dealt with these decisions. We didn't even put it on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Go ahead. I cut you off.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, we had a lot of problems on the ground which we had to solve. And then this was not obligatory. That's what I made a mistake before. This was not obligatory for us, and simply we couldn't waste time and examine what crisis staff is trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was there ever a concern within Novi among members of the crisis staff that if you didn't follow these conclusions and decisions, that you would be punished, that you would be sanctioned?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you know the defendant in this case, Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I did know him in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How is it that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, I was a member of ARK Assembly. I saw him there. And of course, on the television, newspapers. From time to time, I heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you aware that he was the president of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I were aware. It was public.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What was -- did he have any power? During May, June, and July of 1992, did he have any power, any authority, any competence in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really think that he's not a powerful man, or he is without any power.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. What about the ARK Crisis Staff? Did it have any power or authority or competence in your municipality during May, June, July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a body which was not considered seriously, not only in my municipality, also in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was the opinion that you just expressed that it was not considered seriously, was that just your opinion? Or did other people in your municipality share your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a common opinion from I think all people involved in any activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have an indication of how long Your Honours will sit this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to make it very clear to you, if you don't understand the question and you find difficulty in answering in English, please, please answer in your own language because I don't want there to be any misunderstanding, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. If you prefer, we can switch to my native language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you about Mr. Pasic. Is he alive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where is he these days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: He's in Bosanski Novi. He's working in Prijedor, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there would be no difficulty if anybody wanted to call him to this Court in finding him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no any difficulty for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Pasic was the president of the Assembly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic was the president of the crisis staff in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe, but I think in one period of time the president of executive board was the president of the crisis staff in that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In the period --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In the particular period between April 1992 and September 1992, was Mr. Pasic the president of the crisis staff in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe he was. Even I must say that maybe in one period of time, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you yourself - I'll come back to the crisis staff - were a member of that crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the person who has the greatest knowledge of that crisis staff and of the dealings with UNPROFOR, in particular, is Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an address for Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in this moment, but it's a very small place. You can find him very easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we were to ask you overnight to make inquiries, would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Inquiries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be able to find out by making a telephone call what the present address of Mr. Pasic is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would be able, but again, it's not a problem at all for anyone to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may be. But sir, I'm going to ask you very kindly if the Trial Chamber agree that you do that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham is going to do that for you, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I understand she might be interested in his appearance before this Tribunal, but I don't think this is really beyond this or relevant to this area of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think with your experience, you know exactly where Ms. Korner is heading. It's not just what you said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And with all due respect, Judge, I don't think it's his job to do their work to find a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see. Obviously, I'm not going to force the witness to go and look for the address of Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't force the witness either, Your Honour. I'm only inquiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have done this before myself, Ms. Korner, so I know exactly what you are up to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm making sure that Mr. Cunningham understands, I'm making the point that the witness who would have appeared to have been able to give the most relevant information to this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- is Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, if you are able to do, would you be prepared to make a phone call and provide for us a telephone number and an address for Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am able, if you need, I can do that, but it came on my mind that that I've heard that Tribunal already contacted Mr. Pasic, and he is in contact with I don't know whom from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may be so, sir. If you forgive me, if you don't mind doing it, then as I say, I would be very grateful if you would do that and let us know tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's nighttime. It's a little bit inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I have told him that while he's a witness here, after he testifies, that he is not to talk to anyone, not to mention that he's here. And I'm placed in a quandary, if the Court wants him to do that, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Court doesn't want him to do anything. But you're free to accommodate Ms. Korner if you can and if you are willing, and Ms. Korner, I think, will pass on the address to Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we need -- Your Honour, may I say, for various reasons - sorry, I've just been given a note - I don't think we need trouble the witness with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, sir. Can I now return to your own involvement with this case. Mr. Cunningham told us during the course of his examination with you that you met with him about a month and a half ago. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before that, had you met with any other member of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just met once the lawyer, local lawyer who is I suppose a member of the team who just asked me whether I'm willing or not to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can you remember who that was? Was it Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Peric ask you whether you could provide any documents that would assist in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask me about any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you provided documents to the Defence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I bring two documents which I was given from the municipality, and I couldn't find anything else because I don't have any personal archive or documents or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean before you met with the Defence, you went to the municipality to obtain some documents?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not go to the municipality. I asked my friend who is working there just for one document because I remembered very well that we discussed about problems, such problems. And I wanted to remind my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What problems? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: All the problems in -- about people in the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you gave the Defence two documents concerned with the stadium and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the course of the meetings of the crisis staff, minutes were taken. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It should be the case. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was no organisation, was there? No formal meeting of organisation that went unminuted?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I suppose that should be, but I don't know whether anyone took minutes or not on the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the conclusion of the crisis staff's work, a report had to be made to the municipal assembly, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On its activities.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you now, because it means there were some minutes because the assembly confirmed some steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The assembly was obliged to verify the decisions that had been made by the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Where is that report?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: You think documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, where is the physical report that was delivered to the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't work in assembly. If assembly adopts or confirms something, it should be in archive in assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where are the minutes that were taken of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those minutes should have been in the municipal building. That's right, isn't it? Archived.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The records of official meetings of the assembly and/or the crisis staff which took over its functions had to be kept, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Records about assembly meeting should be. I'm not sure for the meetings -- meetings of the crisis staff. Whether or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But we're going around in circles slightly, sir. A minute ago you agreed with me that in order for a report to have been given to the assembly, there must have been minutes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There should be some conclusions or something like that. But you're asking me, if I'm right, are there documents in the assembly building? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you make any attempt to obtain from the assembly -- from the municipal building or anyone who works in the municipality copies of those records?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. If you allow me, I will explain why. I was president of the municipality board, and I was interested just for that exact case that the local SDS has discussed that problem and has concluded something about the situation. I did not have my personal documents or archives, and that's why I was interested just in that. I don't think that I should have anything else apart of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand. But you told us that you asked for copies of documents that were related to the football field, although you've told us a moment ago that was nothing to do with you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that is nothing to do with me, but my responsibility is that board of the SDS, and I was interested what we have concluded in that time. That's why I asked for that -- such document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you knew, didn't you, before you even spoke to Mr. Cunningham, that this case was about the operation firstly of the regional crisis staff, and secondly of the crisis staff in Bosanski Novi. You realised that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I realise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So why didn't you ask someone in the municipality to provide you with copies of the crisis staff minutes of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very simply, I'm not in charge of that. And you know, if I come to assembly and ask for some documents, anyone will ask me, "Who you are to ask that?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you haven't the faintest idea why those documents apparently are no longer at the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that they are no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if they are there, Mr. Dejanovic, I would be most grateful again if you could make a phone call asking whoever is in charge to give them to us.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not capable for that any more. I'm not living in that municipality. I think the Prosecutor's Office has enough capacity to obtain those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can assure you, sir, that the request was met with the explanation that these documents were not there. All right. Can I now, please -- one further thing, sir. Were you staying in the same hotel as the previous witness, Mr. Vidic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did stay, because I saw him when he left hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you know Mr. Vidic before this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. He was member of ARK Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the two of you discuss the evidence that he had given?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure. Hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so it's your opinion, formed by yourself, that the ARK Assembly, as you described it, was an unserious organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And not as a result of any discussion that you had with Mr. Vidic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. It's my expression from that time. Not only mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this description that you gave us of Hyde Park, everyone coming and going, and everyone voting, you never discussed that with Mr. Vidic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Give me the example, maybe I can say what I am remembering, but there was a lot of examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You told us that you became the -- you joined the SDS in 1991 because of what had happened to your family in World War II. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not just because of that. As I explained, it's quite more wide. Not just because of what happened to my family, because of a lot of things. The most important thing was that I believed that with my presence in the SDS, I will try and I will do something in order to prevent some more extreme people to do something, and not because of what happened to my family, but especially because of our historic experience in Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The SDS in its numbers contained some very extreme people, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Vukic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give -- I'm not ready to give any, let's say, opinion about was he extremist or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you don't think that making speeches about what should happen to the babies of mixed marriages was extremist?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that he talked very hard, but still I can't say that he was extremist. I'm not sure that is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, what do you call an extremist?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Extremist is someone who would really do something, something like that. That's my opinion. Maybe I'm wrong, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you think that it is extreme to say that the Muslims and Croats should be driven out of the places where they had lived because it was Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is an extreme statement. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you heard Mr. Brdjanin make a number of statements like that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: He has talked quite hard also, as Mr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't catch --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you mentioned, Mr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm now talking about Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Brdjanin and Dr. Vukic made similar types of speeches, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They talked very hard. That's what I can say. Very hard, very hard statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the effect of those statements, was to terrify, wasn't it, the non-Serbs, in particular, the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it could terrify on some level, but it was not -- still, I can say that they will do the same thing what they -- there was a lot of hard talks from all sides in that time. I can only consider what Mr. Brdjanin and Vukic said in that sense, that there was a lot of hard talks from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not arguing with you at all about that, sir. But at the moment, I'm just concerned with the effect that the speeches made by high-ranking SDS members would have on the non-Serb population. The answer was, wasn't it, that they were terrified, and that's why they began to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, Your Honour, because that's, in effect, two questions. One, were they terrified? And two, is that why they left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's stick to whether they were terrified or not first, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought he'd answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The effect of these speeches by high-ranking members of the SDS was to terrify the non-Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They felt fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the fear was that if they didn't leave, they would be driven out by force? That's what it was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean that it doesn't mean that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, why do you think they were terrified?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were -- they felt fear, but it still doesn't mean that they will be driven out if they don't go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then what were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were afraid of what could happen, as we all were afraid, that some bad things could happen. But it still doesn't mean that they should go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But what bad things would happen as a result of those speeches?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I agree they felt fear. But I think you told that some things could happen as a result of speech. It couldn't be results of speech. It could be results of war circumstances. They felt fear that the war could come and they could be wounded or robbed or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The war had nothing to do with speeches by Mr. Brdjanin and Dr. Vukic that non-Serbs should leave.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was war already there. Combining those speeches and war, it's reasonable for some people to feel fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the other thing about those types of hate speeches, and they were hate speeches, weren't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say they were very hard and strong speeches. I still can't say that they were hate speeches.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But the other problem with making speeches like that is this, isn't it, that the ordinary Serbs began to hate and fear their Muslim and their Croat neighbours, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I consider myself as ordinary Serbs, it's not the case. I didn't start to hate or to fear anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But no doubt when you talked to the farmers, the people who worked on the factory floor, and I'm talking now about Serbs, members of your party, did you notice that they were now also making threats against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm talking about my surrounding, about place where I was living and so on, I can't say that these speeches influenced very much people around me. And I think we confirmed that later on in our relations with non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking now about Bosanska Kostajnica, which was a tiny part, wasn't it, of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But having in mind a situation in my surrounding, I think no one should start to hate someone because of someone's speech. And I'm not sure the speeches were something what produced -- what was the major thing in all what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it is not within your experience at all that what I would call racist rhetoric has any effect on the ordinary person?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you are dealing with people on the ground, I think we could prevent that that speeches became, as you say -- to have major effect on the ordinary person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you say you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the person, you know. Some person may be could listen some speech and start to change their mind. But if we are on the ground working with the people, and tell, okay, the situation is like that and that, we can prevent all this effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you saying that within Bosanski Novi, you were able to nullify, if I can put it that way, any kind of effect that these speeches might have had?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me; I didn't understand the word "nullify".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neutralise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neutralise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He understands that better coming from near the Mediterranean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you and other members of your party were able to ensure that those speeches didn't have that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I did my best, and people with me did the best they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you saying that you are unaware of any situation where local Serbs not in the army, not in a particular paramilitary formation attacked their non-Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you put there also criminals, then I would agree with your answer. No one apart from paramilitary situations and criminals and as you say army, I'm aware were not attacking their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about Serbs who acquired weapons, neither criminals, nor really paramilitaries in that sense that we mean, in the Japra Valley and attacked their neighbours. You're saying you were unaware of anything like that happening?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As my knowledge is, the problems in Japra Valley have been made by paramilitary groups. That's my knowledge. I'm pretty sure it's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I understand what was your last or one of your last answers about this. You are saying, are you, that any shelling, shooting, or any kind of attack was carried out by paramilitary groups? Is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: What my opinion is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were there in the area, you were part of the government of the area, sir. Now, are you saying that all attacks upon non-Serbs were carried out by paramilitary or criminals?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, excuse me, but I'm not part of government. I was president of local SDS party, and it's not government. I think, I really think that these attacks was carried out by the paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you were president of the SDS. Under the Dzeric regulations or the Serbian Government regulations, you were a member of the crisis staff. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was the member of the crisis staff. I attended to the meeting of the crisis staff more because I came from Kostajnica, and Kostajnica was a pretty separate municipality. And having in mind that someone should attend and take care about this part of the municipality, I attended to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the instructions from the Serbian government in Bosnia-Herzegovina about crisis staff included the fact that the president of the municipal SDS board should be a member?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about instructions which I've told you I've never seen. And I was not attended to the crisis staff meetings according to that instructions. I was attending according to instructions from Mr. Dzeric. He didn't notice that presidents of SDS should attend, but it was...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have a delegate from Bosanski Novi attending the -- well, first of all, was there somebody from Novi on the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Grbic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there also a member of -- a delegate to the assembly from Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Three of them, two Serbs and one Bosniak, if we are talking about Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No -- well, first of all the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Two of them were in Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you saying that neither Mr. Grbic or either of the two members of the assembly, the Serbian, ever told you about or gave you a copy of the instructions that had been issued by the SDS board on the 19th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm positive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So how did you know how to set up a crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The crisis staff has been settled according to the regulation still from former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so you, although -- I'm sorry. I'll start that again. Do you agree that the crisis staff functioned only when the assembly could not meet because there was war or a threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the crisis staff replaced or took over the functions of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But all decisions had to be adopted by the assembly as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that for the time that the crisis staff is in existence, it is the government of the area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you talking about crisis staff in municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It performed the local government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we go back to where I was about how many questions ago. You, for the period that you were on the crisis staff, were a member of the government. Do you agree with that now?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a theoretical question, but I think I was not a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not a theoretical question, sir, it's a question of fact. You were, for that period of time while the crisis staff was in existence and you were on it, part of the government of the municipality. That's the situation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you say so. But still, I think the government is one thing, and the assembly is another thing, and crisis staff is third thing. I was member of assembly. I attended -- again, I attended to the meeting as a man from Kostajnica, attended to the meetings of crisis staff, but I still can't say that I'm member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just two last questions for today: What was your job in Bosanski Novi in this period? I don't think you've told us that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was manager of SDK's payment bureau in that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And then this is the last question: Are you telling this Trial Chamber that you never at any stage received any instructions from the regional crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO DEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can positively say that this regional crisis staff did not send, let's say, any instructions we should implement. Even more, I think this crisis staff didn't even think or didn't even consider a situation in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Thank you, Mr. Dejanovic. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, can I make one request before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the presence in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's easy. I just need the exhibit list from the OTP for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll hand that over and to Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
